content: This document is an updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 2001 and updated in 2003, focusing on the comparison of two surgical techniques for tonsillectomy: dissection and diathermy. Tonsillectomy is a frequently performed surgical procedure, but it remains unclear whether one technique is superior to the other. The objective of this review was to evaluate and compare the morbidity associated with tonsillectomy performed using the dissection technique versus the diathermy technique. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Ear, Nose and Throat Disorders Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, BIOSIS Previews, and ISRCTN. Both published and unpublished trials were considered, with the most recent search completed on October 1, 2010. The previous search update was conducted in 2003. The review included randomized controlled trials involving both children and adults undergoing tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy using either the dissection or diathermy technique. Two authors independently selected the studies, extracted the data, and assessed the risk of bias. Two studies, involving a total of 254 participants, met the inclusion criteria for this review. The overall risk of bias in these studies was low, although pain data from one study were excluded due to an unclear risk of bias. One study compared monopolar dissection diathermy with conventional cold dissection in children, while the other study compared microscopic bipolar dissection with cold dissection in both children and adults. The findings from these studies indicated that the diathermy technique was associated with reduced intraoperative bleeding compared to the dissection technique. However, patients in the diathermy group experienced increased postoperative pain. There was no significant difference in the rate of secondary bleeding between the two techniques, although the statistical power of the studies was insufficient to detect small differences in this outcome. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether one method of tonsillectomy is superior to the other. However, there is some evidence suggesting that pain may be greater following monopolar dissection. The authors emphasized the need for large, well-designed randomized controlled trials to establish the optimal surgical technique for tonsillectomy.
